rule.docs:
# repeated-equality-comparison (PLR1714)

Derived from the **Pylint** linter.

Fix is always available.

## What it does
Checks for repeated equality comparisons that can be rewritten as a membership
test.

This rule will try to determine if the values are hashable
and the fix will use a `set` if they are. If unable to determine, the fix
will use a `tuple` and suggest the use of a `set`.

## Why is this bad?
To check if a variable is equal to one of many values, it is common to
write a series of equality comparisons (e.g.,
`foo == "bar" or foo == "baz"`).

Instead, prefer to combine the values into a collection and use the `in`
operator to check for membership, which is more performant and succinct.
If the items are hashable, use a `set` for efficiency; otherwise, use a
`tuple`.

## Fix safety
This rule is always unsafe since literal sets and tuples
evaluate their members eagerly whereas `or` comparisons
are short-circuited. It is therefore possible that a fix
will change behavior in the presence of side-effects.

## Example
```python
foo == "bar" or foo == "baz" or foo == "qux"
```

Use instead:
```python
foo in {"bar", "baz", "qux"}
```

## References
- [Python documentation: Comparisons](https://docs.python.org/3/reference/expressions.html#comparisons)
- [Python documentation: Membership test operations](https://docs.python.org/3/reference/expressions.html#membership-test-operations)
- [Python documentation: `set`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/stdtypes.html#set)

analysis.summary: Flags repeated equality comparisons like 'x == a or x == b' that can be rewritten using a membership test.
analysis.fixDescription: Rewrites repeated equality comparisons of the form 'expr == val1 or expr == val2 ...' into 'expr in {val1, val2, ...}' when all values are hashable, otherwise into 'expr in (val1, val2, ...)'.
hazards: The expression on the left-hand side may have side effects (e.g., a function call), causing it to be evaluated multiple times in the original but only once in the fix.
If any compared value is unhashable (e.g., a list or dict), the fix uses a tuple, but the original may rely on short-circuiting to avoid evaluating later values after a match.

The fix evaluates all values in the set/tuple upfront, which can raise exceptions during construction (e.g., division by zero in a literal) that would not occur in the original if earlier comparisons succeeded.
Comments attached to individual comparison operands may be lost or misplaced during the rewrite into a single expression.
If the left-hand expression is mutable and changed between comparisons (e.g., via aliasing), the original may see different values while the fix uses a single evaluated value.
In rare cases, custom __eq__ implementations may behave differently when invoked multiple times vs. once due to state changes.
The fix may alter operator precedence interactions if the original expression was part of a larger boolean expression relying on short-circuiting for control flow.
If the compared values include duplicates, the deduplication in a set may change behavior if equality is not idempotent or if duplicates had semantic meaning (though unlikely).
